title: POC weekly sync - KV cache fallback and rate policy review
summary: Weekly POC sync focused on a recent spike of 5xx/timeouts traced to cache miss storms and fallback routing to a lower-capacity model. Discussed mitigations: cache warm/writes, request hashing, adaptive backoff, per-customer concurrency limits, and getting VPC flow logs + sample traces for postmortem. Action items include running an isolated burst test, sharing security docs, and proposing a tuned rate policy for the next rollout.
next_steps: SE to run 10k request burst test with k-v cache warmed and share results by 2026-08-16
Customer to provide 30 sample 5xx traces and VPC flow logs by 2026-08-15
Redwood to propose adjusted rate policy (per-customer concurrency + token window) and send config by 2026-08-18
Schedule deep dive on model fallback logic with SREs (tentative 2026-08-19)
Share SOC2/HIPAA attestation and network diagram with Alex Kim by 2026-08-14

Marcus Green - Upload 30 representative 5xx traces and VPC flow logs - 2026-08-15

transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-08-12 09:30 PDT | Duration: 58m
Attendees: Lena (Redwood AE), Samir (Redwood SE), Diego (Redwood CSM), Karen (NovaHealth CTO), Marcus (NovaHealth SRE), Priya (Product), Alex (Security)

[00:00] Lena Ortiz: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh quick agenda — root cause recap from last week, validation tests, proposed rate policy, security docs. We'll try to keep this tight.
[00:22] Karen Liu: Thanks Lena. We saw another burst on friday where latency popped and we got a cluster of 502/504s. Marcus has the traces but, uh, curious what you all saw on your side.
[00:35] Marcus Green: Yeah the dashboards show a cascade starting around 14:07 UTC, queues spiked, the instance pool fell over to fallback model and then we hit capacity and 5xx. We also noticed a bunch of KV cache misses - looked like a cache stampede?
[00:55] Samir Patel: Right, first pass from our end is it's a cold-KV-cache storm. When the prefix TTL expired, many concurrent requests missed and each request tried to rebuild the KV set, which increased load. The routing policy then degraded to a smaller, cheaper model variant to keep latency SLOs but that model didn't have the same throughput and started returning 502s under the burst.
[01:18] Priya Rao: So two parts: the cache rebuild and then the fallback model being underpowered. Is that correct?
[01:24] Samir Patel: Correct. Also there was some interplay with our adaptive throttler - it temporarily allowed many inflight requests because the rate window slid open then closed, causing backpressure.
[01:38] Marcus Green: I remember we saw more CPU on the frontend aggregator too, so maybe we had amplification from retries? Customer-side client retriers were set pretty aggressive.
[01:50] Lena Ortiz: Yeah we noted that, some SDKs default to 5 retries with low backoff which isn't ideal during cache rebuilds. We recommend exponential backoff + jitter and a retry budget.
[02:05] Alex Kim: Quick security note — while we tune this please remember we need preserved audit logs, and network diagram for our Security Ops. SOC2/HIPAA is a blocker until we see attestation and the egress flow.
[02:18] Diego Marquez: Noted, Alex. We'll share the compliance pack and network topology.
[02:26] Samir Patel: For mitigations we propose — one, warm the KV cache proactively for hot prefixes during rollout windows; two, request coalescing for identical prefixes; three, a short-term routing fix: raise the fallback model capacity threshold so we don't turn on the smaller model too early; four, implement an adaptive per-customer concurrency limit.
[02:48] Karen Liu: For warming, can you do deterministic pre-warm for our top 100 prefixes? We can provide the key list.
[02:55] Samir Patel: Yes — we can do a pre-warm job. We'll need the prefix list. Also we'll run a warmed vs cold burst test to quantify the diffs.
[03:08] Marcus Green: On logs — I'll pull and upload the 30 traces, plus the VPC flow logs you asked for. Might be noisy, but we can filter.
[03:18] Priya Rao: Curious about cost impact. If we raise fallback threshold and keep more requests on the larger model, will our token costs spike?
[03:28] Samir Patel: There is a cost delta, yes. But we can do a hybrid: prefer larger model but only for requests that exceed our per-request latency threshold and keep a token budget guardrail. Also intelligent batching during warm windows can reduce unit cost.
[03:44] Lena Ortiz: Also, quantization profile for your model variant could reduce token compute by X-20% depending on sequences — we'll include a recommended quant config in the followup.
[03:56] Marcus Green: Can you explain the adaptive per-customer concurrency?
[04:02] Samir Patel: Sure. Basically set a dynamic limit per customer API key derived from a sliding token-window and observed error rate. If error rate climbs, the limiter reduces concurrency and provides a 429-type signal to preserve stability rather than 5xx. It's like graceful degradation.
[04:20] Karen Liu: We like graceful degradation more than opaque 5xx. But we also need observability - what signals will we see?
[04:27] Samir Patel: We'll emit metric hooks: inflight_requests_by_key, cache_miss_rate, fallback_activation_count, and a 'graceful_throttle' metric when we start returning 429s. We can add dashboards in the Console.
[04:40] Alex Kim: On the compliance side, please ensure the logging mechanism doesn't leak PHI. Marcus, that ties to your retention policy.
[04:48] Marcus Green: Yep we'll scrub identifiable fields before sending logs.
[04:52] Lena Ortiz: Action plan — Samir will run the warmed vs cold burst test, Marcus uploads traces, Alex and Diego will coordinate compliance docs. We'll reconvene after the tests.
[05:02] Karen Liu: One other item — client retry behavior. We'll update SDK config to use backoff with max retries 2 and base 200ms jitter.
[05:12] Priya Rao: Do you recommend any immediate quick fix so we don't see another incident while we wait for the pre-warm?
[05:18] Samir Patel: Yes, two quick fix knobs: lower the fallback activation sensitivity (so model variant switching is less aggressive) and enable a short token-window rate cap (e.g., 30 concurrent tokens per key). These can be toggled in the routing policy quickly. We'll produce an exact JSON to apply.
[05:36] Lena Ortiz: We'll share that JSON as part of the rate policy suggestion.
[05:40] Diego Marquez: Also propose an experiment: run a controlled 10k request burst from our infra with warmed cache and with the new routing policy to confirm improvement before rolling to prod.
[05:51] Samir Patel: Yep, we'll coordinate test harness and share logs. We'll also capture p50/p95 latency and backend 5xx rate.
[05:58] Alex Kim: Last security ask — please include KMS key lifecycle notes and whether logs ever touch third-party analytics services.
[06:06] Lena Ortiz: We'll include that in the compliance pack.
[06:10] Karen Liu: Sounds good. Thanks team.
[06:13] Lena Ortiz: Thanks all, we'll follow up with the test plan and the rate policy JSON.
[06:16] Meeting end.

Notes on transcript: some words auto-transcribed (K-V cache, KV cash) and timestamps are approximate. There is occasional crosstalk and filler words omitted.
